checks.claim: Orthonormal windows and K≤L ensure projected C has full row rank.
checks.explanation: Orthogonality in the full radial function space does not imply independence after a finite projection. An orthonormal window can lie entirely in omitted modes, making its projected row zero despite having enough retained coordinates.
checks.demonstration:
Let $K=6$, $m_p=1$, and let the six columns of $C$ retain radial orders $1,3,5,7,9,11$. For $k=1,\ldots,6$, choose the omitted orders $n_k=11+2k$ and windows
$$w_k(r)=\sqrt{2(n_k+1)}\,R_{n_k}^{1}(r).$$
Radial Zernike orthogonality gives $\int_0^1w_iw_jr\,dr=\delta_{ij}$, while every retained moment $\int_0^1w_kR_n^1r\,dr$ is zero. Thus $K=L=6$, but the $6\times6$ projected matrix is zero and has rank zero.

This also gives a counterexample within the physical affine-pose domain. The two vectors
$$p_{\pm}=(1/2,0,0,1/2,\ \pm1/\sqrt2,0)$$
are unit normalized, have coordinates in $[-1,1]$, have the same invertible linear part $A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)$, and have different translations. Both retained pose encodings are zero. Here $L$ counts the actual columns in Equation (10).

The windows meet the two stated sufficient conditions: radial orthonormality and enough retained modes. They are not asserted to be generated by the particular two-Gaussian construction. That separate family needs a proof or direct check of projected rank; orthonormality alone cannot provide it.
checks.repair: Require and verify full row rank of the projected matrix, or construct the windows inside the retained span with a positive smallest singular value. Use a right inverse for a rectangular matrix.
checks.scope: The implication from radial orthonormality and $K\leq L$ to finite projected rank. The rank of the particular two-Gaussian/Gram–Schmidt implementation is not determined by this counterexample.
checks.claimContext: The finite pose encoding projects $K$ radial windows onto $L$ retained Zernike modes. Section 3.5 treats radial orthonormality and $K\leq L$ as sufficient for the projected matrix to have full row rank.
checks.title: Orthonormal radial windows can lose rank after projection
checks.whyItMatters: An advertised sufficient condition for exact finite pose inversion is missing a finite-span/rank hypothesis.

checks.demonstration:
Equation (9) multiplies each bare radial moment by $\pi\sqrt{(n+1)/\pi}$. The next paragraph defines $C_{n,m_p}^{k}=\int_0^1w_kR_n^{|m_p|}r\,dr$ without that factor. With row-vector stacking, the relation is
$$A=pCD,\qquad D_{nn}=\pi\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{\pi}}=\sqrt{\pi(n+1)}\quad(m_p>0).$$
As a coefficient-wise probe, set $m_p=1$, $n=1$ and $w(r)=2r$. The bare moment is $1/2$, but its multiplier in the normalized coefficient is $\sqrt{\pi/2}$. This isolates one summand of the linear coefficient identity; it does not treat a scalar as a complete physical affine pose.

Inserting $D_{99}=\sqrt{10\pi}$ gives the correct equality.

checks.claim: Eq.45/46 assigns the same π angular prefactor for all m=±mp, including zero.
checks.explanation: When the angular frequency is zero, both terms from the cosine expansion contribute to the same mode. Their sum is twice the value used in the piecewise formula. The nonzero angular bands are unaffected.
checks.demonstration:
Euler's formula gives the angular integral
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(m_p\theta)e^{-im\theta}\,d\theta=\pi\bigl(\mathbf1_{m=m_p}+\mathbf1_{m=-m_p}\bigr).$$
For $m_p>0$, exactly one indicator contributes at either supported mode. For $m_p=m=0$, both contribute, giving $2\pi$. Equations (45)–(46) merge these two coincident contributions into one.

For a coefficient-wise probe, $w=\sqrt2$ has unit radial norm and bare moment $1/\sqrt2$. Its unnormalized zero-mode coefficient per unit pose coordinate is $\sqrt2\pi$; Equation (45) gives only $\pi/\sqrt2$. This is a one-coordinate coefficient calculation, not a complete scalar physical pose.

A physical six-coordinate instance uses $w_k=\sqrt{2(2k-1)}R_{2k-2}^{0}$, with the constant window assigned to coordinate $5$, and the other five windows assigned bijectively to the remaining coordinates. For the valid unit affine pose $p=(1/2,0,0,1/2,1/\sqrt2,0)$, only coordinate $5$ contributes to $n=m=m_p=0$. Equation (41) then gives $a_0^0=\pi$, whereas Equation (45) gives $\pi/2$. Applying the same Zernike normalization to both preserves that factor of two.
checks.repair: Keep the sum of the two indicators, or handle the zero band separately with the doubled angular factor.
checks.scope: The zero-frequency angular integral and its coefficient formula, including a six-dimensional physical-pose instance. Nonzero angular bands retain the stated angular factor.
checks.claimContext: Equations (45)–(46) assign the angular factor $\pi$ whenever $m=\pm m_p$, without treating $m_p=0$ separately. The zero angular band is allowed by the displayed joint coefficient family.

checks.claim: Euclidean norm of Eq.11 equals L2 norm of the corresponding field difference.
checks.explanation: A real cosine field has equal coefficients in both angular bands. The one-sided vector drops one copy, so its unweighted squared norm misses a factor of two even when there is no radial truncation error. Linearity alone does not establish isometry.
checks.demonstration:
Take $m_p=1$ and six radially orthonormal windows. Use the valid normalized physical affine poses
$$p_{\pm}=(1/2,0,0,1/2,\ \pm1/\sqrt2,0).$$
Their difference is $\sqrt2e_5$, so the field difference is $\sqrt2w_5(r)\cos\theta$ and has squared disk norm $2\pi$. A real cosine field has equal normalized complex coefficients in the two angular bands. Parseval therefore gives
$$\sum_{n\geq1}|a_n^{1}(p_+)-a_n^{1}(p_-)|^2=\pi.$$
Any finite positive-band vector has squared norm at most $\pi$, so it cannot equal the field norm squared $2\pi$. This argument applies to any radially orthonormal windows, including orthonormalized Gaussian windows.

For an explicit finite example without a radial tail, choose
$$w_k(r)=\sqrt{4k}\,R_{2k-1}^{1}(r),\qquad k=1,\ldots,6,$$
and retain radial orders $1,3,5,7,9,11$. Only the coefficient at order $9$ changes between the two poses, by $\sqrt\pi$. Hence the unweighted stored distance squared is exactly $\pi$, while the field distance squared is $2\pi$. The projected pose matrix is full rank in this example, so this metric defect is independent of the rank issue.
checks.repair: For positive angular bands, multiply the stored orthonormal coefficients by \(\sqrt2\), and restrict exact isometry to fields contained in the retained radial span. Alternatively retain the full normalized two-band coefficient sequence and state the Parseval identity with its truncation residual.
checks.scope: The exact unweighted one-band isometry claim under Equation (9), including valid six-dimensional affine poses. The reported linear correlation is compatible with a constant scale factor.
checks.claimContext: Equation (9) uses normalized complex Zernike coefficients of a real cosine pose field. Equation (11) stores only the positive angular band. The text calls the resulting unweighted coefficient distance an exact isometry of the disk pose-field space.
checks.title: The one-band pose vector is not an isometry with the disk field
checks.whyItMatters: The mathematical geometry of the advertised embedding is misstated; a weighted finite-span version is available.

checks.claim: Storing geometry separately suffices to recover pose from the phase-modulated joint coefficients.
checks.explanation: Pose phase disappears wherever the geometry carrier is zero. The unit disk has only a constant geometry coefficient, so distinct valid affine poses can have the same constant pose coefficient and identical joint encodings, even when geometry is separately known.
checks.demonstration:
Work at $\beta=1$. The unit-disk geometry has $z_0^0=1$ and every other Zernike geometry coefficient zero. For any six radial windows, write the constant pose coefficient as the linear functional
$$a_0^0(p)=\sum_{k=1}^6q_kp_k.$$
Choose a nonzero translation $b\in\mathbb R^2$ with $\|b\|_2=1/\sqrt2$ and $b\perp(q_5,q_6)$. Such a vector always exists; if both moments are zero, any translation of that norm works. The poses
$$p_{\pm}=(1/2,0,0,1/2,\ \pm b_1,\pm b_2)$$
are unit normalized and have the same invertible affine linear part $A=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)$ but different translations. They have equal $a_0^0$. Every other phase-modulated coefficient is zero because its geometry carrier is zero. Thus the complete joint encoding and the separately stored geometry are identical for two distinct valid physical poses.

The argument uses no special window family, no rank defect, and no phase-wrapping ambiguity. It therefore also applies when the standalone pose measurement matrix has full rank and the windows come from the Gaussian construction.
checks.repair: Require full column rank of the pose map restricted to nonzero carriers and an injective phase range on the allowed poses. Otherwise store pose information separately; storing geometry alone is insufficient.
checks.scope: The geometry-known direction of joint pose recovery, for arbitrary six-window families and valid normalized affine poses. Recovery of geometry when pose is retained is a separate direction.
checks.claimContext: At the neutral setting $\beta=1$, joint encoding multiplies each geometry coefficient by a pose phase. The invertibility paragraph says that retaining either geometry or pose separately suffices to recover the other.
checks.title: Known geometry does not restore pose through zero carriers
checks.whyItMatters: The unconditional side-information recovery statement fails on a standard allowed geometry and valid affine poses.

checks.demonstration:
Let the clean two-bit sequence satisfy \(P(X=00)=P(X=11)=1/2\), and mask each bit independently with probability \(1/2\). Choose an allowed factorized denoiser that copies visible bits and predicts each masked bit by a fair coin. Conditional on \(X\), each resulting bit of \(Y\) differs from its clean value with probability \(1/4\), independently.

Consequently, \(P(Y=00)=P(Y=11)=5/16\), while \(P(Y=01)=P(Y=10)=3/16\). The posterior probabilities \(P(X=00\mid Y)\) are \(9/10,1/10,1/2,1/2\) for \(Y=00,11,01,10\), respectively. The exact tokenwise likelihood optimum predicts these posterior marginals independently at the two positions. Averaging its generated clean pairs over \(Y\) gives
\[P(\widehat X=00,01,10,11)=(7,3,3,7)/20.\]
Re-noising masks each generated bit with probability \(1/2\). The probabilities of the four fully visible latent states are therefore
\[qR(00,01,10,11)=(7,3,3,7)/80,\]
whereas the true latent marginal has
\[q(00,01,10,11)=(10,0,0,10)/80.\]
Both distributions have the same balanced one-bit marginals, so their single-mask and double-mask probabilities agree. Their total variation distance is \(\|qR-q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=3/40>0\). \[\|qR-q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq\mathbb E_Y\!\left[\|p_\phi(\cdot\mid Y)-P(\cdot\mid Y)\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\right].\]
